name: Apple cider vinegar whitening

lead: Apple cider vinegar whitening means rinsing the mouth with ACV to lift stains and brighten the teeth. It is a common natural-remedy suggestion.

Proponents say acetic acid dissolves stains and kills bacteria. ACV is roughly 5% acetic acid and also contains malic acid. No clinical trials of this use were found, and acids can also dissolve tooth mineral.

paras: People swish diluted or undiluted ACV around the mouth briefly, or apply it to the teeth, then rinse with water. It is used occasionally as a natural add-on to normal brushing. Users describe a cleaner feel and report gradual brightening.
Enamel erosion is irreversible and can expose sensitive dentin. Dental sources note that frequency of acid exposure matters and that brushing immediately after acid is discouraged.

web.title: Apple cider vinegar for teeth - Healthline

angle.text: Users swish apple cider vinegar as a natural rinse to dissolve stain and brighten teeth, crediting its acetic acid. It is a low-cost kitchen routine for a whiter-looking smile. No trials of it as a whitener exist, and reference sources list enamel erosion as a known risk of excessive vinegar intake.

lead: Apple cider vinegar (ACV) whitening is a home practice of swishing diluted or undiluted apple cider vinegar around the mouth, or applying it to the teeth, with the aim of lifting surface stains and brightening the smile. People use it as a low-cost kitchen alternative to whitening strips and trays, and it circulates online as a natural whitening rinse.[1]

ACV is about 94 percent water and roughly 5 percent acetic acid, with a small amount of malic acid from the apple juice. Proponents argue that its acidity dissolves stains and that its antibacterial reputation helps keep the mouth clean.[1] Healthline reports that a 2014 laboratory study found apple vinegar, white vinegar and hydrogen peroxide all had bleaching effects, and describes the evidence for ACV's dental benefits as limited.[1]
Dentists and reference sources link acidic rinses to enamel erosion and dentin sensitivity.[1]
infobox: About 94% water, 5% acetic acid, malic acid
Peroxide whitening, which oxidises pigment molecules

paras: Users describe gargling or rinsing with ACV, sometimes diluted in water, sometimes mixed with baking soda and sometimes followed by brushing.[1] Proponents argue that the acidity dissolves stains, and some credit its antibacterial reputation.[1] Wikipedia notes that major health organisations and regulators do not recommend ACV as a therapy and that there is no high-quality clinical evidence for its other popular health claims.

ACV is made by fermenting apple juice to cider and then converting the ethanol to acetic acid with acetic acid bacteria; unfiltered versions can retain the "mother", a cellulose-rich biofilm. It is used in dressings, marinades and as a preservative, and brands differ in acid content.

Wikipedia describes tooth whitening products as most commonly based on hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide, oxidising agents that break large pigment molecules into smaller ones that reflect less light. This mainly targets intrinsic stains, while extrinsic stains can often be removed by cleaning, micro-abrasion or whitening toothpaste. Baking soda is described there as a low-abrasive stain remover, and the article notes historical remedies, including honey, burnt salt and vinegar suggested by the medieval surgeon Guy de Chauliac, and barbers who applied acid to teeth, which was effective but eroded enamel.

No studies found of ACV as a tooth whitener in people. Healthline reports a 2014 laboratory study in which apple vinegar, white vinegar and hydrogen peroxide each showed a bleaching effect, and a 2022 study of 190 extracted teeth in which vinegar and apple cider caused the most enamel erosion of the substances tested.[1] A 2023 laboratory study found 5 percent acetic acid performed similarly to a sodium hypochlorite mouth rinse against oral bacteria.[1]
A 2020 systematic review of ACV consumption generally found diluted, moderate intake appeared safe, but it did not study tooth whitening.

Dental erosion is the irreversible loss of tooth structure to non-bacterial acid. Items with a pH below roughly 5 to 5.7 can trigger it, vinegar-pickled foods are implicated, and swishing acidic liquids increases widespread erosion. Dentin hypersensitivity can follow when acid wears away enamel and exposes dentin; guidance includes not brushing immediately after acid exposure. Healthline adds that erosion can increase sensitivity and decay risk, that swallowing undiluted ACV can burn the throat, and that ACV may interact with diuretics, digoxin and diabetes medications.[1]

Wikipedia's ACV article lists enamel erosion from excessive intake, increased dentin hypersensitivity, burns from topical use on skin and irritation or corneal injury from eye contact, and warns against mixing vinegar with chlorine bleach. For comparison, peroxide whitening itself commonly causes sensitivity, and enamel surface changes have been reported with it.

Healthline advises consulting a dentist or doctor before using ACV for whitening.[1] For peroxide whitening, the US FDA endorses gels up to 6 percent hydrogen peroxide or 16 percent carbamide peroxide, EU retail hydrogen peroxide is limited to 0.1 percent with up to 6 percent allowed under professional supervision, and dental guidance recommends an examination and cleaning before whitening.
ACV is among the natural whitening routines shared online alongside baking soda, oil pulling and charcoal.[1]

lore.intro: ACV is passed around online as a natural whitening rinse, usually in lists of kitchen remedies for a brighter smile.[1]
